Bite Me
BITE mee
interjection, phrase (Gen X slang)
American teen slang by the mid-1980s, common through the 1990s in schoolyards and on television: a rude dismissal meaning "get lost; I don’t care what you think." It is generally taken as a clipped form of coarser imperatives; its exact origin is uncertain. The verb bite is Old English bitan.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Bite me is the Gen X way to slam a door with two words. A parent asks a question, a teacher gives a correction, a sibling makes a remark, and the answer is: "Bite me." It means, roughly, "I reject you and everything you just said," with a coarse edge most teenagers understand even if they could not explain it. The Christian observation is that Scripture uses the same picture, and uses it as a warning. "If ye bite and devour one another, take heed that ye be not consumed one of another" (Gal 5:15). Biting is what animals do; Paul says that a church, or a family, that speaks this way will eat itself alive. God’s instruction for the moment of irritation is the reverse: "Not rendering evil for evil, or railing for railing: but contrariwise blessing" (1Pe 3:9). "A soft answer turneth away wrath: but grievous words stir up anger" (Pro 15:1). "If it be possible, as much as lieth in you, live peaceably with all men" (Rom 12:18). And the apostle puts this kind of speech on the list of things a Christian strips off like old clothes: "anger, wrath, malice, blasphemy, filthy communication out of your mouth" (Col 3:8). Christ, who had every right to dismiss us, says instead, "Come unto me" (Mat 11:28). A father should be plain: this one goes. Not because it is the worst thing a child could say, but because it is contempt in a short sentence, and contempt has no place in a home that has been shown grace.

Webster 1828 Definition

Gen X rude dismissal (by the mid-1980s) meaning "get lost; I reject you"; Scripture uses the biting image as a warning — if ye bite and devour one another, take heed (Gal 5:15).

expand to see more

BITE ME, interj. (Gen X slang, mid-1980s–1990s, United States) A rude dismissal: get lost; I don’t care what you think. "Clean your room." "Bite me."

Generally taken as a clipped form of coarser imperatives; origin uncertain. Kin to eat my shorts and talk to the hand.

Common in 1990s sitcom and cartoon dialogue as the stock teenage retort.

Webster 1828: BITE, v.t. preterit tense bit; participle passive bit, bitten. 1. To break or crush with the teeth, as in eating; to pierce with the teeth, as a serpent; to seize with the teeth, as a dog. 2. To pinch or pain, as with cold; as a biting north wind; the frost bites. …

Decode for parents: this one is contempt with a coarse edge; it belongs on the list of things a Christian puts off (Col 3:8).

Key Scripture

Gal 5:15 — "But if ye bite and devour one another, take heed that ye be not consumed one of another."

1Pe 3:9 — "Not rendering evil for evil, or railing for railing: but contrariwise blessing; knowing that ye are thereunto called, that ye should inherit a blessing."

Pro 15:1 — "A soft answer turneth away wrath: but grievous words stir up anger."

Rom 12:18 — "If it be possible, as much as lieth in you, live peaceably with all men."

Col 3:8 — "But now ye also put off all these; anger, wrath, malice, blasphemy, filthy communication out of your mouth."

Modern Corruption

Bite me is contempt in two words, most often aimed at parents; Scripture warns that those who bite and devour one another are consumed, and commands blessing for railing.

expand to see more

Contempt at the door. The phrase is short because contempt does not need many words. It dismisses not an argument but a person, and in Gen X homes it was most often fired at mothers and fathers. That gives it a special weight, because the fifth commandment does not lapse at thirteen. A child who learns to answer correction with bite me is learning to answer God’s correction the same way. Put it off with the rest of the old man’s wardrobe (Col 3:8).

Families that bite. Paul’s image is exact: biting and devouring until there is nothing left (Gal 5:15). Homes are rarely destroyed in one blow; they are eaten away by a thousand small dismissals. The cure is the gospel’s contrary pattern — blessing for railing (1Pe 3:9), the soft answer (Pro 15:1), and peace as far as it lies in us (Rom 12:18) — learned from the Savior who answered our rebellion with His own life.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Old English bitan (to bite) → mid-1980s teen dismissal bite me (origin uncertain) → 1990s sitcom staple; Scripture: if ye bite and devour one another, take heed (Gal 5:15).
